text: WHEN an instruction is saved with an effectiveTo, the system SHALL reject the save unless effectiveTo is after effectiveFrom.

comments.text: R2 constrains the Data model (it names a bean, a field or a choice value), but the Data model's 'Rules the table cannot carry' list does not cite it. Add an R2 entry there, or say why it is omitted, so the two sections agree on which rules live outside the table.

text: Abstract polymorphic base — never stored on its own; every instruction carries exactly one of its subtypes.

comments.text: The data model note says the base is 'never stored on its own; every instruction carries exactly one of its subtypes', but the derived set declares SettlementMethod as an embeddedBean with no persistence, while BankTransfer, CustodyAccount and CashSweep are each full persistence.entities with their own tables and sheets. These two facts do not fit together: an embedded part lives inside the embedding row, so it cannot 'carry' one of three separately persisted subtypes, and a polymorphic ref to one of three entity tables is not something the field kinds shown obviously express. Please state the carrying mechanism — e.g. three optional refs plus an exactly-one exclusivity rule (which, like P1, the bean table cannot carry and would need a requirement), or make the subtypes embedded too. Without it, an implementer cannot tell what 'exactly one subtype' means at the row level.

text: A3 (verifies R3): WHEN the selection of a settlement instruction for a new trade is listed, the system SHALL omit retired instructions.

comments.text: R3 and A3 regulate a surface this spec does not contain: the selection of a settlement instruction happens in the trade booking flow, which Scope explicitly pushes out ('Changes to the trade booking flow beyond excluding retired instructions from selection'), and no trade bean exists in the Data model. As written it is unclear where the exclusion is enforced and what artifact A3 would be demonstrated against. Either state that the exclusion is a filter on the ref picker over SettlementInstruction (and say so), or record it as a requirement handed to the trade-booking specification — otherwise A3 cannot be executed within this spec's deliverables.

text: The uniqueness rule the table cannot carry is P1 (one active instruction per counterparty and currency).

comments.text: The note concedes the platform cannot carry P1, which leaves R1's check-then-activate as the only enforcement. Two concurrent activations for the same counterparty and currency can both pass R1's check and both commit, leaving two active instructions and violating P1's 'at any time'. For a settlement register this is a real money-moving defect, not a theoretical one. Add a requirement (or state the mechanism) that makes the conflict check and the status change atomic, so P1 holds under concurrent activation.

text: the effectiveFrom/effectiveTo ordering rule, and the exclusion of retired instructions from new trades.

comments.text: The effective dates are stored and ordered (R2) but never used: R3 excludes only retired instructions from selection, so an instruction whose effectiveTo has passed — or whose effectiveFrom is still in the future — remains status active and therefore selectable for new trades. Either that is intended (status is the sole gate and the dates are informational, in which case say so) or a requirement is missing that selection also respects the effective window. As written, the dates invite the reader to assume window-based exclusion that no requirement delivers and no criterion tests.

text: A persistable refdata.SettlementInstruction entity with a draft → active → retired lifecycle.

comments.text: The lifecycle is stated as draft → active → retired, but the spec never says whether retired is terminal. R1 only refuses activation when another instruction is active, which reads as permitting retired → active; if retirement is meant to be irreversible (the usual reading for a register whose rows existing trades keep pointing at), that should be stated, since it changes what R1's activation check must cover and what the edit form may offer. A one-line clarification resolves it.

text: Considered, none apply: authorization (platform default — any signed-in user), performance, volume, availability, audit (platform audit trail), locale, cost.

comments.text: Constraints records authorization as 'platform default — any signed-in user', which means any signed-in user can create, activate, retire, and edit any instruction — including editing the bank/account details of the one active instruction for a counterparty while trades settle against it. Nothing in the requirements says whether an active instruction's method fields may be edited at all (versus requiring retire-and-replace), or whether activation and retirement should be restricted to a narrower role. For a register that drives actual payments this is a permission path worth deciding explicitly rather than inheriting by default; even one sentence stating the intended rule (or confirming open editing is intended) would close it.

text: Later the instruction is retired; from then on it no longer appears when a new trade's settlement instruction is chosen, while existing trades keep pointing at it.

comments.text: The six open threads cover the polymorphism mechanism, the P1 race, R2's citation, A3's surface, the unused effective window and whether retired is terminal — but none covers the active state's editability. The scenario establishes that trades keep pointing at an instruction after it is retired, which implies the row's contents are what payments rely on; yet nothing says whether an ACTIVE instruction's method fields and contacts may be edited. As written, any signed-in user can change an active instruction's bank details or contacts in place, silently redirecting future payments with no retire-and-replace step. Either state that active instructions are immutable and replacement goes through retire-then-create (which also strengthens the audit story the Constraints section leans on), or state explicitly that in-place edits to active instructions are permitted. One sentence resolves it; without it, the edit form's behaviour on an active row is undefined.

text: R1: WHEN an instruction is activated, the system SHALL refuse the activation while another instruction for the same counterparty and currency is active

comments.text: R1 gates only the activation event, but activation is not the only path to two active instructions for the same counterparty and currency. A plain save that changes the counterparty or currency on an already-active instruction can collide it with another active instruction (e.g. instruction A active for (CP1, USD); editing A's currency to EUR while B is active for (CP1, EUR)) — P1's 'at any time' is then violated and no requirement or criterion covers that save. Either extend the one-active check to any save that changes counterparty or currency on an active instruction (with a matching criterion), or state that active instructions are immutable in which case the path closes — but the spec should not leave this save path unregulated while claiming P1 as an invariant.

text: The edit form shows status as a status badge

comments.text: The lifecycle is the spine of this spec, yet only one transition guard (R1) exists and the permitted transitions themselves are never enumerated. The UI renders status as a read-only badge, so nothing in the spec says how a draft becomes active or retired — a dedicated action on the form, or a status edit? — and whether draft → retired directly, or active → draft, are legal moves. R1's 'WHEN an instruction is activated' is only defined for the draft → active path the scenario describes; for every other transition the behaviour is undefined and no criterion could test it. This is distinct from the open thread on whether retired is terminal (that concerns retired → active only): enumerating the full allowed transition set, and stating where each transition is performed, closes both this gap and gives that thread a concrete place to land.

text: Embedded polymorphic subtype of refdata.SettlementMethod — serialized as JSON into SettlementInstruction.method together with its subtype discriminator; never a root entity, no table of its own.

comments.text: The new notes resolve the carrying-mechanism question by making the three subtypes embedded JSON parts, but the derived set still declares each of BankTransfer, CustodyAccount and CashSweep as a persistence.entity with 'its migration and table' and its own observer.sheet — directly contradicting 'never a root entity, no table of its own'. Since the derived block is regenerated from the bean blocks, this reads as the subtype bean blocks still being declared as persisted entities (or the derived set being stale). Reconcile them: if the embedded-JSON mechanism is the intent, the subtype bean blocks need to be declared as embedded so the derived set regenerates to embeddedBean entries with no tables or sheets; if the tables are intended, the notes need to change back. As written, an implementer gets two opposite instructions from the same document, and the sheets listed for the subtypes are surfaces the notes say should not exist.
